paragraphs.text: The Proposition of Photinus the Manichaean and the Reply of Paul the Persian. "If contraries are never said [to be contrary] to themselves [?]..." [The manuscript] gives: "Proposition of Photinus the Manichaean. Refutation by Zacharias, bishop of Mitylene. Beginning: Contraries are not said to be contrary to themselves," etc. Who [?]

If "above" is a substance, then "below" must also be a substance; and again, if "above" is an accident, then "below" must also be an accident. How, then, if the good is opposed to the wicked and the wicked to the good, and the noble to the evil and the evil to the noble, is it not necessary that, since the good exists, the wicked also exists, and since the noble exists, the evil also exists? And again, if the good or the noble is a substance, then the wicked and the evil are also a substance; and if one of them is an accident, the other is an accident too. For if the good or the noble exists, but the wicked or the evil will not exist, to what can the good or the noble be opposed, when its counterpart neither exists nor can be spoken of in relation to it? That is absurd. And how is the division that sets the good against the wicked true, if the one exists and the other does not? But if this is so, as the truth bears witness and the argument has shown, how are they not lying who say that there are not two ungenerated principles, one good and one wicked, one noble and the other evil? And if those who abolish the two principles are lying, how is it not necessary for those who are eager to live with the truth to teach two principles?

Answer. Anyone who wishes to prove, from the contrariety of evil to good, that there are two ungenerated principles ought, before everything else, to have laid down and defined what the good is and what evil is, and how many distinctions there are of good and of evil, and only then to begin on his premises. Whoever does not do this neither refutes nor establishes anything, but spends his words to no profit. Since the questioner has not done this, he lays down an undefined premise, from which two syllogisms arise, as follows: Evil is opposed to the good; everything that is opposed to something exists; therefore there is an ungenerated and evil principle. Again: Evil is either a substance or an accident; everything is either a substance or an accident; therefore there is an ungenerated and evil principle. But he ought to have constructed the first syllogism like this, if anyone were in fact saying that evil does not exist: Evil is opposed to the good; everything that is opposed to something exists; therefore evil exists. Then, taking this whole argument as proved, he should have reached his conclusion by a further construction, like this: Evil is either without beginning or comes from something else. Does it come from something good or from something evil? From something good it cannot; therefore evil comes from evil. Since, then, principles must be ungenerated, and the good cannot be the principle of evils, one must conclude that the ungenerated principle of evils is evil. In the same way he should have taken the whole of the second syllogism and established his conclusion through another syllogism. But the questioner passes over all this, and under the pretence of a double syllogism, or rather a fourfold one, argues as follows. Let it be set out once more,

to still greater laughter: Evil is opposed to the good; everything that is opposed to something exists; therefore there is an ungenerated and evil principle. Bravo for the precision of one eager to live with the truth! In his hands the ambiguous term becomes univocal; the occasional becomes universal; the division of opposites produces the things it distinguishes; and whatever simply exists becomes an ungenerated principle. The syllogism as a whole is as contrary to its premise as, by their account, the evil principle is to the good. And so that I may not seem to be slandering him, I will make this plain. The good is spoken of in two ways: one eternal, the other generated. Evil is likewise spoken of in two ways: one in the proper sense, the other in name only. Each of these is also said in many ways, but I am not yet dealing with that. The questioner, however, takes them without distinction, or rather applies the whole to the eternal ones, saying something like this: "If the good is opposed to the wicked, and the wicked to the good", without having said what sort of good or what sort of wicked he means. Further, evil is opposed to the generated good, since it comes about by deliberate choice, but it is not opposed to the eternal good; yet he takes this too as universal, though it is particular. Further, from the fact that evil is set over against good and good against evil, he concludes that they coexist with one another, saying: "For if the good exists but the wicked will not exist, to what can the good be opposed?", as though it were impossible for something to exist first and only afterwards to be set over against another. Again, having established that evil exists, he immediately goes on to treat it as eternal and coexisting with God, saying: "But if this is so, as the truth bears witness, how is it not necessary to teach two ungenerated principles?" Further, when he ought to have concluded from the premises given that evil exists, he concludes: "Therefore there is an ungenerated and evil principle." How so, my friend? As if whatever exists must also be a principle, and whatever exists must also be ungenerated! What then shall we do with plants, the various animals, grammar, rhetoric, philosophy, and the other natures and arts, not to list them one by one? Or do you not shrink from saying that these too, since they exist, are ungenerated principles? And then how are there two ungenerated principles, and not many? And what becomes of the august religion of the Manichaeans, if there are many principles and not two ungenerated ones? But let it be granted that none of the contraries is opposed to itself, but each to its own counterpart; let it be granted that the paired members of things set over against each other are substances or accidents; let it be granted that evil exists and is opposed to the good; let the division between them also be true. How do you get from this to teaching two ungenerated principles? What did you say in your first premises? What necessity did you lay down from which this follows? He says that evil exists because it is opposed to the good. But there are many things that exist and are opposed to one another: burning fire to drowning water, as you say, and water to fire, the moist to the dry and the dry to the moist, corruption to generation and generation to corruption. Yet you do not on that account call them many ungenerated principles. How then is it possible for all these, though by nature contrary to one another,

[?] to come from one principle, but not for the good and evil as opposites? Besides, how is it, my companion, that you did not notice the inquiry of nearly all the ancient sages into evil? They granted that it exists and that it is opposed to evil [?], but disputed with one another about how it exists or where it comes from. That is what they did; but for you the existence of evil has been taken for its "when" [?], and being opposed to something for its "how"; or rather, for you the whole has been [?] into one.

What has been said would be enough to answer what was proposed. Nevertheless I have drawn up some chapters. Some grant that evil is opposed to the good, but show that evil is neither an ungenerated principle nor coexistent with God; others show that evil is not opposed to the good; some prove that even on the basis of what the Manichaeans say it is not necessary to teach two ungenerated principles; and others set out necessary teaching about good and evil [?]: whether it is one thing for something to exist and another for something to be opposed to something.

1. To be something is a matter of the thing in itself; to be opposed is a matter of its relation to another. What is in itself exists before what is in relation to another, and what is in relation to another exists after what is in itself. [?] How is it necessary, because the wicked is opposed to the good and the good to the wicked, that they coexist with one another? And if it is not necessary, how is it necessary, because they are opposed to one another, to teach two ungenerated principles? For ungenerated principles must coexist with one another.

2. If, just as knowledge of opposites comes about by setting the opposites side by side, so also the existence of opposites comes about by setting side by side the things distinguished, how will opposites not be causes of one another? And if opposites are causes of one another, how will the good not be the cause of evil, and evil of the good? That is absurd.

3. If the existence of opposites will come from setting the opposites side by side, how does the division of contraries compel the opposites to coexist with one another?

4. If God knows things present and past no better than things that are yet to be, how is it impossible for him to be set over against things that are yet to be, just as he is against things present and already past? [?] And if it is not impossible for God to be set over against things that are yet to be, how is it necessary, because evil is set over against the good, that evil be ungenerated?

5. The ungenerated, that is, the eternal, is prior to the generated, and the generated, that is, what at first was not but later came to be, comes afterwards; and the ungenerated is set over against the generated. If so, how was the ungenerated not in some sense set over against the generated not yet present, before anything generated existed? If it is possible for the ungenerated in some sense to be set over against what has not yet come to be, how is it impossible for the eternal good in some way to be set over against the wicked that does not yet [?] exist?

6. That which is without beginning is prior to what has a beginning, and what has a beginning comes later; and what is without beginning is set over against what has a beginning. If so, how was it not in some way so set over before anything with a beginning existed? And if it is possible for what is without beginning in some way to be set over against what has a beginning but is not yet present, how is it impossible for the noble, the ungenerated, in some sense to be set over against an evil not yet present?

7. "Good" and "ungenerated" differ in meaning: the one signifies a state possessed, "ungenerated" a privation. In this they differ from each other; but in the manner in which they are set over against their opposites they do not differ at all. For in the case of God, "ungenerated" is set over against its opposite in just the same way as "good" is.

8. If it is possible for generated things, as generated, and for things with a beginning [?], as having a beginning, to be eternal, then it is also possible for the eternal, as eternal, to be generated and to have a beginning. But if the second is impossible, the first is impossible too.

9. If, according to you, no known coming-to-be ever takes place without soul, and soul is not always in matter, how can coming-to-be be eternal, when it does not take place without soul?

10. If coming-to-be with soul is one kind and coming-to-be without soul another, and the one with soul is known while the one without soul is unknown, how is he not drawing his proofs from unknown things, when he proves his thesis from a coming-to-be other than the known one?

11. If God was ungenerated when generated things did not exist, and without beginning when things with a beginning did not exist, then he was also good when the wicked did not exist, and noble when evil did not exist. And if he was set over against generated things when generated things did not exist, and against things with a beginning when they did not exist, then, even though the wicked and evil did not exist, he was set over against the wicked and the evil.

12. If it is possible that God, before generated things existed, was ungenerated but not set over against things with a beginning, then it is also possible that before the wicked existed he was good but not set over against the wicked; and that before evil existed he was noble but not set over

13. If it is fitting that God, being good, should of necessity be set over against his own evil, and being ungenerated, against the things that come into being from him, then it is far more fitting that he be set over against the things that will come into being through his making, and from him through choice.

14. If, according to you, the elements come from one principle, and yet they are opposed to one another, how is it necessary, because of the antithesis of contraries, that there be two ungenerated principles? For these, although by nature contrary to one another, come from one matter.

15. If good is opposed to evil, and evil to good, just as the elements are opposed to one another, [?] both will be from [one] principle.

1. If they are opposed as generation and corruption are, they will be the beginning and end of some underlying subject.

2. If the two principles are opposed to one another as light and darkness are, they take each other's places in turn.

3. If evil is opposed to good, and good to evil, as disease is to health, they will be states of a single subject.

4. If the principles are opposed to one another as white and black are, they will be accidents of some subject.

5. If the two principles are opposed to one another as virtue is to vice, they will be the right action or the failing of some subject.

16. If, then, the two principles are opposed to one another neither as the elements are to one another, nor as generation and corruption, nor as white and black, nor as light and darkness, nor as disease and health, nor as virtue and vice [?]. For these are the ways in which opposites are opposed in our experience.

17. If the wicked principle of the Manichaeans is opposed contrarily to the good principle, but not contrarily to the things that come from it, then it is at peace with the things that come from it and at war with the good principle. And if so, how are the things that come from it contrarily opposed to one another? For nothing that is at peace begets from itself things that are at war with one another.

18. If none of the opposites is opposed to two contraries, how is the evil principle, which is one, contrarily opposed both to the good principle and to the things that come from it?

19. If the saying is true, as indeed it is, that contraries are opposed not to themselves but to one another, how, according to you, is the evil principle opposed to itself? And if none of the contraries is opposed both to itself and to another, how is the wicked principle opposed both to itself and to the good? For then there will be a principle from a principle, which

20. If it does not befit God to make contraries for the needs of the things that come into being, how does it befit him to beget from himself [?] for his own need? And if one who makes things for the needs of others lacks nothing, while one who does so for his own need is in want, how is the god of the Manichaeans not in want, since he begot for his own need, as they say?

21. Suppose the evil principle shares with the good principle both being, and when it is, and where it is, just as fire shares with water both being and being an element, and is opposed to it only in respect of evil and good, as fire too is opposed to water only in respect of heat. Then both principles will come from one principle; for fire and water too come from one principle

22. If none of the contraries orders its partner, whether by necessity or out of need, but the good principle ordered matter by necessity, then matter is not [?] contrary to the good principle. And if matter is not
23. If the pairing of contraries necessarily makes both [?] plain, they will not come from contrary principles. For as far as they stand apart by nature, so far are they united by

24. If plants and animals come into being from the contrariety of the elements, but nothing comes into being from the contrariety of the principles, then the principles are not opposed to one another as the elements are, as you say.

25. If evil, though taught to coexist with God, is not held in equal honour with God, because even among generated things there are things equal in honour [?], and things short-lived by nature are more honourable than long-lived ones [?], how will there not be something prior to the ungenerated that ordered the principles as ungenerated?

26. For all generated things are governed according to the order the Maker established. Where life is not immortal, death is opposed to that life; and where the good is not unchangeable, evil is opposed to that good. But where life is immortal, death is not opposed to that life; and where the good is unchangeable, evil is not opposed to that good.

27. Things whose existence comes by generation also have their good by nature [?]. Where the good comes by creation, evil comes by contrariety; but where the good is by nature, [evil] [?] does not come by contrariety.

[28.] If the eternal good wills the eternal evil to exist, then it wills evil itself to be eternal too. But if it does not will it to exist, and yet it exists, and the good knows it, then the eternal good suffers something against its will. [Therefore] it will not have evil as its contrary, for nothing that has a contrary is wholly free from suffering.

29. What sort of good does the questioner know, to which he says the wicked is opposed? And what sort of wicked does he understand, to which he claims the good is opposed? Then generated things are ungenerated! But if they are ungenerated, let him show that temperance is ungenerated, and continence, and justice, and likewise adultery, fornication and pederasty. But if they are generated, how is it necessary, because the wicked is opposed to the good of generated things, that the wicked also

be opposed to the generated [?] good of God?

30. If what follows upon generated things necessarily follows upon God, and there follow upon generated things, for example, generation, corruption, want, sin, and in a word passions, how will these not follow upon God as well? But if what follows upon generated things does not necessarily follow upon God, how is it necessary, because evil is opposed to the noble in generated things, that evil also be opposed to the noble in God?

31. If God is a good and ungenerated principle, and the evil principle is also a god, as you say, and these attributes do not follow upon both, how is it necessary for them to follow both upon the ungenerated good and upon the generated?

[?] becomes the beginning of evil, and the cessation of evil is often the beginning of good, then God's good, which is as unchangeable as it is ungenerated, will not [?] have an opposing evil.

33. If evil is nothing other than a swerving to the other side, and God is free from this, how will he be opposed to something he does not possess?

34. Suppose the good and the wicked are present in generated things by virtue of the substance of preexisting principles, just as hot and cold are present in natural things from the preexisting elements. Then the substances from which the good and the wicked come will come from one principle. For water and fire, from which come the heating and the cold, come from one principle, according to you.

35. If the noble and the evil are present in generated things by participation in preexisting principles, how do we judge those who have failed to deserve punishment, and those who have acted rightly to deserve enjoyment? And if we have evil by participation, how is it that we judge someone with a fever to deserve pity and sympathy, but an informer to deserve blame and punishment?

36. If no one has ever forbidden by law the things that happen in nature necessarily, by participation in preexisting things, since these happen of necessity, how is it that both divine and human laws forbid injustice and impiety?

37. The evils forbidden by law, for which punishment has been fixed, such as blasphemy, injustice, and in a word impiety and sin, never take place without soul. If so, how is the soul not the cause of the evils forbidden by law, for which punishment has also been fixed? And if the soul is the cause of the evils forbidden by law, how are the evils forbidden by law not from the soul? And if this is so, how does the questioner have knowledge of what exists, whence

38. If we sin without willing it, and are justified without choosing it, how is it that we are punished as though we had sinned by will, and enjoy good things as though justified by choice? And if each comes about by will, how is each not from will?

39. If acting by natural necessity is better than working with unforced freedom, then matter, which acts by natural necessity, is better than God, who works in freedom. But if acting by necessity is worse than working without compulsion, how do the Manichaeans not cut human beings off from what is better, when they deprive them of free choice?

40. According to the Manichaeans, the blameless God is blameworthy because he brought into being those who did evil, though he knew them beforehand. If so, then in truth the god of the Manichaeans is blameworthy, because he emitted from himself the sons who acted impiously, though he knew them beforehand. And if the god of the Manichaeans foreknew the impieties of his own sons and still emitted them, and yet in emitting them is not the cause of their impieties, how is the one who foreknew, according to

[?] in truth God [?] the transgressions of those who would come to be, and in bringing into being those who would commit them, is he the cause of the transgressions? 41. If the good God had made human beings unable to do either good or evil, and he himself were the one who carried out both in them, then God would be the cause of human goods and evils alike. But if he made human beings able to do either, then they themselves are the causes of both.

42. The good is spoken of in two ways: the good in the God who truly is, and the good in created things. The good in the God who truly is is again understood in two ways: by nature and by making. By nature it is what displays the excellence of his essence; by making it is what is seen in the creation and providence of the things that exist. The good in created things is good in some cases by nature, in others by [?] position, and in others for the sake of usefulness. By nature, as the created works themselves are good, for the good seen in creation is the same as the good in the nature of created things. By use, as with wealth, office and poverty; that is why such things sometimes become evils and sometimes do not. By choice, as with piety and righteousness and, in a word, virtue. For the sake of usefulness, as with the snake insofar as it does harm, fever, famine, punishment for sins and the like, since these train us in piety. Evils too are spoken of in two ways: some properly so called, others by name only. Properly so called are things like impiety and sin; by name only are things like the snake, famine, fever, punishment for sins, earthquake and things similar to these. In truth these are goods, since they train those who suffer them toward piety, but we reckon them evils. In the same way bloodletting and taking medicine are reckoned evils by those who undergo them, but in truth they are goods. For of goods, some are good for their own sake, and others for the sake of what comes about through them.

THE BLASPHEMIES OF THE MANICHAEANS. 43. Since these things are so, the Manichaeans dishonor the good that displays the excellence of the divine essence, by making it out to be equal to evil and representing it as needy and weak. The good seen in the creation and providence of the things that exist they take away from the good God, calling his benefaction evil. They insist that our nature and our needs belong to the evil principle. Whatever leads us to virtue or makes us better they slander as an outflow of evil. And they declare virtue itself and vice to be a numbness of nature, not the fruits of the will. Now if, in teaching these things, they are eager to live in company with the truth, then let the Manichaeans too be counted nurslings of the truth; but if the opposite is the case, let each person draw the conclusion for himself. 44. If the good is a substance, then the good person will certainly be an accident; and if evil is a substance, the evil person will be an accident. But if the good person is a substance, the good will be an accident; and if the evil person is a substance, evil will be an accident. The same argument applies to the fine and the bad.

By “accident” I mean here not what belongs to substances naturally and of necessity, but what occurs by free choice in the actions of rational creatures. 45. If we must take the most exact knowledge of the truth as our starting point, and Mani’s ungodliness, which brings with it ignorance of where evils come from, has impiety as its foundation, how can those who embrace Mani’s false teaching be anything but lovers of ignorance and impiety?
